issuer: New Mexico Taxation and Revenue Department
title: New Mexico TRD Ruling 495-96-1 Basis of Qualified Equipment for Investment Credit
text:
Ruling 495-96-1
Issued: October 15, 1996
Effective: October 15, 1996
A ruling has been requested concerning the application of certain provisions of the Investment
Credit Act to the following facts:
X is regularly engaged in manufacturing in New Mexico both end products and the
processing equipment necessary to manufacture the end products. The manufacturing takes
place in facilities consisting of real property, improvements and equipment, all of which is
owned by a New Mexico political subdivision (Z) and leased to X under authority of an
industrial revenue bond. The processing equipment which X manufactures is both for use in
X's own end product manufacturing plants and for sale to third parties.
As agent for Z, X has purchased machines, mechanisms and components (“Parts”)
and fabricated and assembled the manufacturing equipment in place within the plant. To
establish the value of the manufacturing equipment or components of the manufacturing
equipment for federal income tax purposes, X capitalized the direct and indirect costs of the
Parts and of the installation, assembly and fabrication of the Parts into the integrated
manufacturing equipment. The capitalized cost of the manufacturing equipment or
components included all direct and indirect costs which are includable in capital
expenditures under the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 for property which is depreciable as
3-, 5-, 7-, 10- or 15-year property thereunder and includes tangible property, materials,
supplies, tools, scraps, spoilage, administration, purchasing, transportation, warehousing,
handling, security, insurance, legal, accounting, rework, permits, carrying charges, taxes and
similar services and expenses incurred in connection with the purchase and production of
the manufacturing equipment.
In 1991, the Taxation and Revenue Department issued Ruling No. 495-91-1 to X
allowing qualified equipment to be valued at its capitalized value for federal income tax
purposes in this situation. (It also addressed other issues.) The law subsequently changed to
incorporate this part of the ruling.
In a corporate reorganization, X has formed a new corporation, Y, and has
contributed to Y all of X's rights, title and interest in the property used by X in its end
product manufacturing operation and its process equipment manufacturing operations. The
contribution of assets to Y was consistent with the provision of the Internal Revenue Code
found at 26 USCA Section 351. Following this Section 351 occurrence, Y will carry on the
manufacturing operations in New Mexico and elsewhere, using the same property and
employees as were previously used by X.
Y requests that Ruling 495-91-1 which was originally issued to X be re-issued to Y. Because of
changes in the provisions of the Investment Credit Act which took effect subsequent to the issuance of
Ruling 495-91-1 and because some provisions of the Investment Credit Act will not apply to Y, the
department cannot issue a verbatim re-issuance of Ruling 495-91-1, but instead will rule on the above facts
as they apply to Y under the current provisions of the Investment Credit Act.
Y asks if the value of qualified equipment for purposes of the Investment Credit Act is the same as
the basis of valuation for federal income tax purposes, which includes all of the capitalized direct and
indirect costs of the machines, mechanisms, tools and components and installation, assembly and

fabrication thereof into integrated manufacturing equipment or components thereof. Y further inquires if
qualified equipment includes all 3-, 5-, 7-, 10- and 15-year property under the Internal Revenue Code which
is an essential machine, mechanism or tool, or a component or fitting thereof, used directly and exclusively
in the manufacturing plant, including by way of example, such things as process equipment, lights, boilers,
air conditioners, computers and peripherals, furniture, office equipment, air compressors, water chillers,
refrigeration equipment, water treatment equipment, packaging equipment, warehousing equipment and
electrical control equipment.
Under Section 7-9A-6 NMSA 1978:
Equipment not previously used in New Mexico and not previously approved for a
credit under the Investment Credit Act that is owned by the taxpayer or owned by ... the
state or a political subdivision thereof and leased or subleased to the taxpayer is qualified
equipment if it is in New Mexico and is incorporated or to be incorporated within one year
into a manufacturing operation. (emphasis added)
Qualified equipment includes any “essential machine, mechanism or tool, or a component or fitting
thereof, used directly and exclusively in a manufacturing operation and subject to depreciation for purposes
of the Internal Revenue Code by the taxpayer carrying on the manufacturing operation...”. (Section 7-9A-3
NMSA 1978). Accordingly, such items as furniture, shelving and supplies are not “equipment”. [3 NMAC
13.6.9 (formerly IC 6:2)]
Because the term manufacturing operation is defined as a plant to produce goods, equipment need
not be employed exclusively in the manufacturing process to be qualified equipment as long as the
equipment is employed in the plant in which the manufacturing process occurs. Therefore for the purposes
of the Investment Credit Act, “equipment” may include, but is not limited to, such items as manufacturing
process equipment, lights, boilers, air conditioners, computers and peripherals, air compressors, water
chillers, refrigeration equipment, water treatment equipment, packaging equipment, warehousing equipment
and electrical control equipment if such items are used directly and exclusively in the plant. [3 NMAC
13.6.10 (formerly IC 6:3)]
The value of qualified equipment until January 1, 1998 “... shall be the adjusted basis established for
equipment under the applicable provisions of the Internal Revenue Code”. (Section 7-9A-7 NMSA 1978)
But, effective January 1, 1998, Section 7-9A-7 NMSA 1978 states:
The value of qualified equipment shall be the purchase price of the equipment unless
the equipment is introduced into New Mexico and has been owned for more than one year
prior to its introduction into New Mexico by the taxpayer applying for the credit, in which
case the value shall be the reasonable value of the equipment at the time of its introduction
into New Mexico; provided that no taxpayer shall for any taxable year claim a value of
qualified equipment greater than two million dollars ($2,000,000).
Because the statute which takes effect January 1, 1998 does not provide any direct guidance on
valuation of self-constructed machinery and equipment, Y proposes using its capitalized value. Y asserts the
capitalized value for purposes of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 for self-constructed machinery and
equipment is analogous to “purchase price” for machinery and equipment bought from another party.
Hence, the department will accept the capitalized value for purposes of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986
as the basis for Investment Credit Act valuation of self-constructed machinery and equipment installed in
the New Mexico manufacturing plant.

This ruling does not address nor does it intend to address the issue of whether X may transfer or
assign any unclaimed or unused portion of an investment credit earned by X to Y.
